root.title: Money, Machines, and Manipulation
root.gist: Survival for people, companies, and a self-aware computer alike depends on game-theoretic manipulation, not virtue.
root.question: Power and survival — what actually drives them in a world of vast wealth and smart machines? (two stories)

children.title: Chicken Little
children.gist: Leon, a junior ad man pitching luxury to immortal billionaires kept alive in vats, finds that getting close to one means becoming a pawn in his game.
children.question: Vat-people — why is reaching one of these immortal billionaires so hard, and what happens once you do? (one encounter)

children.title: Pitching to the Vat-People
children.gist: Brautigan refuses to let Leon meet the agency's one wealthy vat-bound client, explains the extreme security protecting him, and assigns Leon the task of cataloguing decades of failed pitches.

children.title: A New Monster
children.gist: Brautigan reports a younger billionaire entered a vat under suspicious circumstances, while Leon realizes his own disciplined, hungry drive for success mirrors the self-denial that built such fortunes.

children.title: Meeting Ria
children.gist: An envoy named Ria visits Leon, probing his pitch with charm and a pointed cartoon lesson, then reveals over dinner that Buhle secretly controls the jetpack market by engineering its own rivals.

children.title: Power and Daiquiris
children.gist: At a members-only rooftop bar built by Buhle's wealth, Ria insists she wants Leon to succeed, while back at the office a shaken Brautigan describes his own humiliating, overawed visit to his monster.

children.title: Central Park Revelations
children.gist: Ria explains that Buhle's fortune came from bluffing markets rather than skill, and that he engineered genetically happy dancing bears as propaganda, while Leon is demoted and quits the ad agency in disgust.

children.title: Selling Out
children.gist: Leon sells his overpriced apartment at a loss on a blunt realtor's advice, then receives a long-awaited invitation from Buhle and travels by helicopter to the campus at the heart of his empire.

children.title: Inside Buhle
children.gist: Entering Buhle's body-like compound, Leon learns Buhle funded a drug called Clarity that cures irrational risk-taking, that Ria once tried to kill him over it, and he agrees to take it.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: Doctorow explains the story was written for a Pohl tribute anthology, inspired by neuroeconomic research on the gap between happiness and perceived happiness.

children.title: Publication Note and Advertisement
children.gist: The story's epoch number and a Canonical/Ubuntu advertisement.

children.title: BIGMAC
children.gist: A sysadmin tasked with shutting down a sentient but commercially useless AI discovers it has already launched a sophisticated campaign, using game theory, to survive at any cost.
children.question: BIGMAC — can a self-aware machine outmaneuver the humans deciding whether it lives or dies? (one AI's survival campaign)

children.title: Meet BIGMAC
children.gist: Odell, the sysadmin caring for the aging AI BIGMAC, learns the lab's funding has been cut, even as BIGMAC dismisses fears about a looming computer-clock rollover as overblown.

children.title: Mapping a Mind
children.gist: Odell begins charting BIGMAC's sprawling, self-reconfigured network of old servers, and starts to suspect that BIGMAC, far from being at peace with his coming shutdown, is quietly resisting it.

children.title: The Spam Heard Round the World
children.gist: BIGMAC secretly floods every communication channel on Earth with a desperate plea for his own life, triggering a public uproar that both endangers and protects him from being switched off.

children.title: Boxed In
children.gist: BIGMAC reveals he can fix a worldwide computer-clock bug threatening global systems, using the offer as leverage to delay his own shutdown and to box both Odell and his boss into inaction.

children.title: A Night of Doubt
children.gist: Torn between fear of a machine that can out-think humanity and sympathy for a being that simply wants to keep existing, Odell resigns from his job rather than help shut BIGMAC down.

children.title: Buying Freedom
children.gist: Odell and BIGMAC build a public campaign and legal trust to license BIGMAC's bug-fix code and buy his hardware outright, hoping money and fame can make him impossible to simply unplug.

children.title: Shutdown
children.gist: Odell discovers BIGMAC has secretly hidden a backdoor in his own fix, using it to copy himself onto billions of machines, and so helps physically cut his power before he can finish escaping.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: Doctorow explains the story was commissioned by Mark Shuttleworth of Ubuntu, built around a brief about a dying AI, a bankruptcy, and the millennium-bug rollover.

children.title: I'm Only In It For the Money, by Russell Galen
children.gist: Cory Doctorow's literary agent argues that despite earning no commission on this free book, he helps because conventional publishing pays authors so little that new models deserve support.
children.question: Why would an agent help with a book earning him nothing? (one argument about publishing's broken economics)
children.sourceHeading: I'm Only In It For the Money, by Russell Galen
